summary: The note covers several aspects of the Franco-Prussian War (1870–71): a planned French seaborne invasion of northern Germany that proved impossible due to Prussian coastal defences, Prussian military reforms under Albrecht von Roon that increased mobilization, and the war's lasting influence on artillery and staff doctrine. It also describes the armistice period in Paris, the French Navy's abandonment of its blockade, and the war's causes and diplomatic stance, including Bismarck's role and the Government of National Defense's refusal to cede territory.
one_line: Overview of the 1870–71 Franco-Prussian War, covering failed French naval plans, Prussian military reforms, artillery doctrine, and the war's causes and course.
key_facts: The Franco-Prussian War was fought from 19 July 1870 to 10 May 1871 between the Second French Empire and the German states of the North German Confederation led by the Kingdom of Prussia.
Prussia had built coastal defences around the big North German ports, including batteries with Krupp heavy artillery with a range of 4,000 yards (3,700 m), double the range of French naval guns.
The French planned a seaborne invasion of northern Germany to divert German troops and encourage Denmark, with its 50,000-strong army and the Royal Danish Navy, to join the war.
Albrecht von Roon was Prussian Minister of War from 1859 to 1873 and put into effect reforms in the 1860s that integrated the regular army and the Landwehr reserves.

Prussian reforms provided for conscription of every male Prussian of military age in the event of mobilization, so Germany mobilized more soldiers despite France having a larger population than all participating German states.
The Prussian bold use of artillery, silencing French guns at long range and then supporting infantry attacks at close range, proved superior to the defensive doctrine of French gunners.
The French 75 was an artillery piece optimised to provide direct fire support to advancing infantry, reflecting Prussian tactics adopted by European armies by 1914.
The Prussian Army held a brief victory parade in Paris on 17 February; the city was silent and draped with black and the Germans quickly withdrew.
Bismarck honoured the armistice by allowing train loads of food into Paris and withdrawing Prussian forces east of the city, pending payment of a five billion franc war indemnity.
An exodus occurred from Paris as some 200,000 people, predominantly middle-class, went to the countryside.
The Krupp 6-pounder steel breech-loading cannon had a longer range and higher rate of fire than the French bronze muzzle loading cannon, which relied on faulty time fuses.
Historian Dallas Irvine said the French system "was almost completely effective in excluding the army's brain power from the staff and high command."
On 6 September, Favre on behalf of the Government of National Defense declared France would not "yield an inch of its territory nor a stone of its fortresses."
By September 15, German troops reached the outskirts of Paris, and on September 19 the Germans surrounded it and erected a blockade.

Following the capture of most of the professional French army at Metz and Sedan, naval officers were sent to command hastily assembled reservists of the Garde Mobile, and the French navy abandoned the blockade of north German ports for the winter in September 1870.

entities.name: Napoleon III
entities.role: French emperor who planned the seaborne invasion and was captured at Sedan along with French Marines and naval infantry

entities.name: Albrecht von Roon
entities.role: Prussian Minister of War from 1859 to 1873 who put into effect military reforms in the 1860s

entities.name: Otto von Bismarck
entities.role: Prussian chancellor who honoured the armistice and whose ambitions for German unification are cited as a cause of the war

entities.name: Favre
entities.role: Member of the Government of National Defense who declared France would not yield territory on 6 September

entities.name: Moltke
entities.role: Prussian commander whose expectation was that staff officers would show initiative and independent thinking

entities.name: Dallas Irvine
entities.role: military historian quoted on the French army's staff and high command

entities.name: Krupp
entities.role: maker of heavy artillery and the 6-pounder steel breech-loading cannons issued to Prussian artillery batteries

entities.name: Royal Danish Navy
entities.role: navy of Denmark, which the French hoped would join the war alongside its 50,000-strong army

entities.name: Garde Mobile
entities.role: French reservist force to which hastily assembled reservists belonged, commanded by naval officers after the loss of professional officers

entities.name: North German Confederation
entities.role: German states led by the Kingdom of Prussia that fought against the Second French Empire

entities.name: Government of National Defense
entities.role: French government that declared France would not cede territory and renewed the declaration of war

entities.name: Paris
entities.role: French capital besieged by German troops from 19 September, and site of the brief Prussian victory parade on 17 February

entities.name: Alsace-Lorraine
entities.role: region into which a German attack was expected and where Prussian forces were concentrated

entities.name: Metz
entities.role: site of a siege where most of the professional French army was captured

entities.name: Sedan
entities.role: site of the battle where Napoleon III and French forces were captured

entities.name: Battle of Königgrätz
entities.role: battle for which the Dreyse needle gun was famous

entities.name: Russo-Japanese War
entities.role: 1904–05 war whose evidence suggested infantry with smokeless-powder rifles could engage gun crews effectively, largely ignored by most European armies

entities.name: Dreyse needle gun
entities.role: Prussian army rifle, 25 years old at the time, with a range of only 600 m and no rubber breech seal

entities.name: French 75
entities.role: artillery piece optimised for direct fire support to advancing infantry
